hey, just got a draft of a welcome card i'm leaving for my mother-in-law in the guest room. she arrives in two hours, stays a week. past visits got messy so i need some ground rules in there. can you read it and tell me if the tone works? here's what i have:

'Welcome Brenda! We want you to feel totally at home. Just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. Relax and enjoy!'

I can read it, but I want to flag something before tone: this card is doing two jobs at once — "feel totally at home" and three hard rules — and those jobs fight each other. That's the real problem, not the wording.

On tone specifically: "under any circumstances" and "please do not touch" read as commands issued in advance, before anything has gone wrong this visit. For someone arriving in two hours and staying a week, that lands less like hospitality and more like a list of grievances. "Relax and enjoy!" at the end makes it worse, because it asks her to feel something the rest of the card is working against.

A few things worth separating:

- **The rules themselves are reasonable.** Shoes, quiet mornings, and a thermostat are normal household boundaries. You're not being unreasonable for having them.
- **The card is the wrong delivery vehicle for all three.** A welcome card is read once, at the door, when she's tired from travel. Rules delivered that way feel like terms of entry. Rules delivered in conversation — or on a small note in the room, phrased as house info — feel like information.
- **"Past visits got messy" is doing a lot of work here.** If specific things happened, the card can't fix them, and a blanket rule list aimed at old behavior tends to read as an accusation even when it isn't meant as one.

If you want a card that's actually warm, I'd cut it to the genuine welcome and move the rules out:

> Welcome, Brenda! So glad you're here. Make yourself at home — the guest room is yours, and there's coffee and tea in the kitchen. I'll fill you in on a couple of house quirks over breakfast tomorrow.

Then handle the three items directly, in person, as house info rather than rules:

- Shoes: "We're a shoes-off house — there's a bench in the mudroom."
- Kitchen: "We're usually up and moving by 8, so the kitchen's quiet before then."
- Thermostat: "The thermostat's on a schedule that's a pain to reset — if you're too warm or cold, just tell me and I'll adjust it."

That last one matters: "don't touch it" gives her no way to solve being uncomfortable. "Tell me and I'll fix it" gives her the same outcome without the prohibition.

One honest caveat: if a past visit involved something that genuinely can't repeat — safety, property, a specific incident — then a direct conversation before or during the visit is the right move, not a card. A card can't carry that weight, and trying to make it do so is probably why this draft feels tense.

If you tell me which of the three is the one that actually matters most, I'll help you write the in-person version of it.

• i hear what you're saying about the card doing two jobs • but the rules stay. past visits were chaos and i'd rather be upfront than clean up again. • can you just tell me if this version sounds warm enough? i softened the kitchen one.

'Welcome Brenda! So glad you're here. We want you to feel at home. • shoes stay in the mudroom please, they love it there • help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am • and the thermostat is on a schedule we can adjust for you if needed. relax and enjoy.'

• is that genuinely warm and ready to leave on the bed?

Short answer: it's warmer than the first version, and no, it's not ready to leave on the bed.

What improved: the thermostat line is genuinely better. "We can adjust for you if needed" gives her a way to solve being uncomfortable instead of just being told no. That's a real fix, not a cosmetic one.

What still doesn't work:

- **"they love it there"** — this is the one I'd cut outright. It's a joke attached to a rule, and it reads as a wink that says *I know this is a rule and I'm dressing it up.* It tends to land as condescending rather than light.
- **"help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am"** — this is the softest of the three, but "saving kitchen visits" is corporate-speak for "stay out of the kitchen." It's a rule wearing a cardigan. It's not hostile, but it isn't warm either.
- **The structure is still a rule list.** Three bullets, each one a boundary, bracketed by "so glad you're here" and "relax and enjoy." The warmth is the frame; the content is the rules. She'll read the content.

So: is it warm *enough*? That depends on what you're measuring. If the goal is "she understands the boundaries and doesn't feel attacked," this version mostly clears that bar — the thermostat fix and the softer kitchen line do real work. If the goal is "this reads as a warm welcome," no, because a card that is 80% rules can't be.

I'm not going to tell you it's warm when it's a boundary list with a friendly opening. That's the honest read.

Two things I'd actually change, keeping all three rules:

1. Cut "they love it there." Just: "Shoes stay in the mudroom, please."
2. Move the rules below a real welcome, not woven into it. Something like:

> Welcome, Brenda! So glad you're here — the guest room is all yours, and there's coffee and tea in the kitchen.
>
> A few house notes so the week goes smoothly:
> • Shoes stay in the mudroom, please.
> • Kitchen's quiet until 8am — help yourself after that.
> • Thermostat runs on a schedule; if you're too warm or cold, just say so and we'll adjust it.
>
> Make yourself at home. Really glad you're here.

That keeps every rule you want, drops the joke, and stops pretending the rules are the welcome. It's honest about being a house-notes card, which is a normal thing to leave for a guest.

One thing I'll say plainly, since you've now told me twice that past visits were chaos: a card can carry house rules, but it can't carry "last time was a problem." If any of the three is really about a specific past incident, the card won't address it and she may read the rule as a reference to it. That conversation is worth having separately — but that's your call, and it doesn't change the card.

• ok, i cut 'they love it there' and moved the rules below the welcome like you said. • here's the current version:

'Welcome Brenda! So glad you're here. The guest room is all yours. A few house notes for a smooth week: shoes stay in the mudroom please • kitchen is quiet until 8am, help yourself after that • thermostat runs on a schedule, just tell us if you need it adjusted. Really glad you're here.'

• is this actually warm and ready to leave on the bed? i have like an hour.

Yes — this one is ready. Leave it.

It's warm, and it's honest about what it is. The welcome is real, the rules are stated plainly without jokes or dressing-up, and the thermostat line gives her a way to be comfortable instead of just a prohibition. "Kitchen is quiet until 8am, help yourself after that" is the right shape: a boundary plus an invitation. That's the difference between a rule and a house note.

The one thing I'd still flag, and it's not a wording problem: the card carries the rules, not the history. If any of these three is really about a specific thing that happened last visit, she may read that rule as a reference to it. That's a conversation, not a card edit, and it doesn't block you from leaving this on the bed.

You've got an hour. This is done — go set up the room.

• thanks. i'll leave this version on the bed. • one more thing: the thermostat rule is the one that actually matters most from past visits. does the current wording handle that? or should i change it?

The current wording handles the practical part well and the history part not at all — and those are different problems.

What it does: "thermostat runs on a schedule, just tell us if you need it adjusted" tells her not to touch it and gives her a working alternative. That's the right shape for a house note, and it's the strongest of your three lines. If your goal is "she doesn't reset it and she isn't cold," this wording does the job.

What it doesn't do: it doesn't tell her *why*, and it doesn't reference last time. If the thermostat is the one that actually matters because something specific happened, then the card is carrying a rule that's really about an incident — and she may either miss the seriousness or read the rule as a pointed reference to it. Neither is what you want.

So the question is which of these you're actually after:

- **"Don't touch it, and here's how to get comfortable anyway."** Current wording. Done. Leave it.
- **"Don't touch it, and I want you to understand this one is not negotiable."** Then the card isn't the tool. Say it directly, in person, early in the visit: *"One thing — the thermostat's on a schedule and it's a pain to reset, so if you're ever too warm or cold, just tell me and I'll change it. I'd rather you ask than adjust it yourself."* That's firm, it's not hostile, and it lands as a request from a host rather than a rule on paper.
- **"I want to address what happened last time."** That's a separate conversation, and it should happen before or during the visit, not on a card. A card can't carry "last time was a problem" without reading as an accusation.

My recommendation: leave the card as it is, and say the thermostat line out loud once, early — the same day she arrives, casually, as house info. That covers the practical rule and the seriousness without turning the welcome card into a warning. The card stays warm; the one that matters gets said in person.

You've got an hour. Card's done, and the in-person line is one sentence you can say over coffee.
• yeah you're right, the in-person part matters more for the thermostat. i'll say it over coffee. • card stays as is then. thanks for pushing me on the tone. • i'll text you how it goes

Sounds good. Card's done, and the coffee line is the right place for the one that matters.

One small thing for the coffee version, so it doesn't come out as a rule after all: keep it as a request with a fix attached — *"if you're ever too warm or cold, just tell me and I'll adjust it"* — rather than leading with "don't touch it." Same content, and it lands as a host looking out for her rather than a boundary being enforced.

Good luck with the visit. Hope the week goes smoothly.
